profile_website_field:
Profile website field. Create the account, complete any onboarding, then open profile settings or "edit profile".
Put the target URL in the field the guide names (Website, Homepage, URL, Links, About, Bio). If the field is a free-text
bio or about box, write one or two natural sentences and include the full URL (some sites auto-link it) or an HTML/BBCode
link if the guide shows that format. Save, then open the PUBLIC profile page (not the edit page) to verify.
Pitfalls: some profiles are private until an avatar or first post exists; some hide the website field until email is
verified; a few strip links from bios but keep the dedicated Website field.
article_post:
Article or blog post. Create the account, find "New post" / "Write" / "New story". Write a genuine short article, 300 to
600 words, on a topic that fits the keywords. Place the link once in the body on the anchor text, as a real hyperlink
(use the editor's link tool or the markup the guide shows). Add a title, and a category or tags if required. Publish, not
draft. Verify on the published post URL.
Pitfalls: editors differ (rich text, Markdown, raw HTML block); a link pasted as plain text is not a backlink; some
platforms hold first posts for review, report those as unverified with the post URL.
bookmark_submit:
Bookmark or link submission. Find "Add link", "Submit", "Add URL" or "Post". Fill URL, title (use the anchor text or a
descriptive title containing it), description (one or two sentences), category and tags. Submit. Verify on the new
bookmark's page or the listing that shows it.
Pitfalls: many of these are Pligg or Scuttle clones with a captcha at submit; if it appears, report manual. Some show the
link only after a moderator approves, report unverified with the submission page URL.
url_shortener:
URL shortener. Paste the target URL, submit, copy the short link. Verify by opening the short link: it must redirect to
the target or show an interstitial that leads there.
Pitfalls: Cloudflare Turnstile or reCAPTCHA gates on most large shorteners, report manual when present.
page_builder:
Page builder site. Sign up, create a site or page from any template, add a text or paragraph block, write a short
relevant paragraph and insert the link as a hyperlink on the anchor text (or the HTML block the guide shows), then
publish. Verify on the published page's public URL, not the editor.
Pitfalls: unpublished drafts are not live; some builders put new sites behind a "coming soon" page until you turn it off.
forum_post:
Forum post or reply. Register, verify email if asked, then either open the thread the guide names or start a topic in a
relevant board. Write a useful reply or topic of a few sentences and include the link once, on the anchor text if the
editor supports links or as the bare URL. Verify on the thread page.
Pitfalls: many forums block links for new members until a few posts exist; if the link is stripped, report manual with
that note. Do not spam multiple threads.
forum_signature:
Forum signature. Register, open profile or user control panel, find "Signature", add the link on the anchor text using
the forum's BBCode or link tool, save. Then post one genuine reply so the signature appears publicly. Verify on that
post's page.
document_share:
Shared document. Create a document with a title related to the keywords, write a short paragraph, insert the link on the
anchor text, then set sharing to public or "anyone with the link" and publish if the platform has a publish option.
Verify by opening the public share URL in a fresh context.
Pitfalls: view-only public links are fine; links inside a private document are not backlinks.
directory_listing:
Directory or business listing. Use "Add your business" or "Add listing". Fill business name, category, address, phone,
description and the website field with the target URL. Choose the free plan when asked. Submit and complete any claim
step. Verify on the public listing page.
Pitfalls: listings often wait for approval; report unverified with the listing URL when pending.
social_post:
Social post. Sign in, create a public post or message that includes the link with a short relevant sentence. Make sure
visibility is public. Verify on the post's permalink.
qa_answer:
Question and answer. Find or ask a question the target genuinely answers. Write a helpful answer and include the link as
a source. Do not post link-only answers. Verify on the answer's page.
Pitfalls: reputation gates; if links are not allowed yet, report manual.
comment:
Comment. Open an item that relates to the keywords, post a relevant comment of two or three sentences with the link.
Verify on the item page after the comment appears.
pages_site:
GitHub Pages. This one IS a followed link, and it is the difference worth saying out loud: the page sits on the
customer's own github.io site, is indexed like any other page, and passes ranking strength. It is not the same
promise as a Facebook album, so do not describe them the same way.
GitHub is connected once, through GitHub's own device page: a window opens with the code already filled in, the
person approves it, and it is never asked again on that machine. Only public repositories are in reach. If a
call answers needs_connect, connect first and call again.
One repository per website, named after the website, never one per keyword. A row of thin one-page repositories
is what gets GitHub accounts suspended, and the account is the customer's asset in the same way their Facebook
Page was. Everything for one website goes in one repository, at /<keyword-slug>/index.html.
The page has to be an original page about their page: what the thing is, who it is for, what is in it. A copy of
the customer's own page is duplicate content -- it will not rank, usually will not be indexed, and republishing
it is something GitHub will act on. A page that is only a title and a link is not indexed at all on a fresh
site, so the link is never seen and the work is wasted.
The keyword is the anchor text of the link to their page, and the link carries no rel attribute so nothing can
quietly make it nofollow. Their address is repeated as plain text in the footer, which is what a reader checks
before clicking. Nothing is loaded from another domain: no fonts, no scripts, no analytics.
After committing the page, rebuild the repository's index.html so it links to every page in the site -- a page
nothing links to is crawled late or never. Then switch Pages on for the main branch at the root; already on is a
success, not a failure.
Finally, wait. GitHub accepting the commit is not the page serving: the first build of a new site takes a minute
or two and the address 404s until it finishes. It counts as live only when the published address loads for a
stranger and the link is really in it. Offer indexing at that point, and pace the next one -- three a week is an
ordinary site publishing its own writing; more than that on one site is a footprint.
Pitfalls: the repository address is not the published address (github.com/user/repo is a code listing, the page
is at user.github.io/repo/slug/); committing over an existing file without its sha is refused; and a customer
who reinstalls must not end up with a second site for the same website, so the repository is matched by its
homepage field, not by name alone.
media_set:
Facebook media set. This one is bought for traffic, not for ranking strength: the link is a mention Facebook
rewrites through its own redirector, and what it earns is a page on a trusted domain that ranks for a long-tail
phrase and sends the searcher on. Say that to the user rather than counting it as a followed link.
Prepare before touching Facebook: one specific keyword the customer could realistically rank for (call
suggest_keywords on the target page, then pick the narrowest phrase with buying intent, not the broadest);
three to eight screenshots of the customer's own page, each file named for the keyword and what it shows; and a
150 to 250 word description whose FIRST line is the target URL and whose last line repeats it.
The host must be a Page, never a personal profile: albums on profiles are not indexed and profile URLs change
shape. The Page must be published, with no country restriction and no age gate, because each of those puts a
login wall in front of the crawler. A page created minutes ago with nothing on it is a weak host; if it is new,
post two or three ordinary things first.
Build it under Photos, then Albums, then Create album. Title is the keyword written as a title a person would
click, under 60 characters. Paste the description and check the line breaks survived. Set the audience to Public
-- a globe, not a lock. Add the photos, give each one its own caption, put the most descriptive first because it
becomes the cover, and publish rather than saving a draft.
Then take the album's own address, the one containing /media/set/?set=a. -- a /photo/?fbid= address is a single
photo and the wrong page. Strip the __cft__ and __tn__ tracking parameters. Open it in a fresh logged-out
context: if it loads and the description is readable, it is finished; if it asks for a login, a visibility
setting is wrong and nothing else matters until it is fixed.
Finish by submitting the album for indexing and telling the user it usually appears within days and ranks later.
Pitfalls: one album per page per week, never a burst -- Facebook restricts pages for it and near-duplicate
albums get ignored. Never reuse a description with the keyword swapped. Never buy engagement.
other:
Mixed method. Follow the guide steps literally; the PLACEMENT step tells you where the link goes. Verify on the resulting
public page.
